L29@P0: 1. Introduction.-In this note the authors wish to outline a theory of
L30@P0: determinants in a finite factor. This theory originated in an attempt to
L31@P0: prove that the trace' of a generalized nilpotent operator is zero. The
L32@P0: properties of the determinant, which we shall derive, will allow us to prove,
L33@P0: more generally, that the trace of an arbitrary operator lies in the convex
L34@P0: hull of its spectrum.
L35@P0: There is no difficulty in proving that the trace of a proper nilpotent is
L36@P0: zero or that the trace of a normal operator lies in the convex hull of its
L37@P0: spectrum. For arbitrary finite matrices, this latter result is proved by
L38@P0-1: 425MATHEMA TICS: FUGLEDE AND KADISON PROC. N. A. S.
L39@P1: passing to a superdiagonal form of the matrix. From this last remark we
L40@P1: obtain the general result for operators in an approximately finite factor.
L41@P1: These facts did not, however, enable us to deal with arbitrary factors of
L42@P1: type II .
L43@P1: In §2 we define the determinant on regular operators in a factor of
L44@P1: type HII, and state the properties of this determinant. The proof that
L45@P1: the trace lies in the convex hull of the spectrum is given in §3 as an application of the results of §2. The uniqueness of the determinant is
L46@P1: noted in §4. The final section, §5, begins with the justification for considering only positive-valued determinants. The paper concludes with a
L47@P1: study of the possible extensions of the determinant to singular operators
L48@P1: in the factor.
L49@P1: The complete details of the theory outlined in this paper will appear in
L50@P1: a subsequent publication.

L117@P3: 3. Location of the Trace.-In this section we shall apply the theory

L121@P3: is a generalized nilpotent operator in Mt.

L131@P3: 4. Uniqueness of the Determinant.-In this section we shall characterize
L132@P3: the determinant in a factor Mt of Type II, by means of some of the algebraic
L133@P3: properties listed in §2.

L142@P3: defined in §2.
L143@P3: The proof of this theorem proceeds by first showing that A1(X) > 0
L144@P3: and that it suffices to prove A1(H) = A(H) for positive H. This is accomplished by proving that the function T1(A) = log A1(exp A), defined on
L145@P3: self-adjoint A, possesses the properties of the trace. The theorem now
L146@P3: follows from the uniqueness of the trace (cf. R.O. I, Theorem XIII, p.
L147@P3: 219).
L148@P3: 5. Related Questions.-In this section we shall indicate the reasons

L151@P4: discuss the possibilities of extending the determinant to the singular
L152@P4: operators in M.
L153@P4: Concerning the first of these questions, it is natural to ask whether or
L154@P4: not a notion of determinant can be developed which, in the finite-dimensional case, reduces to the usual determinant. In this connection, we
L155@P4: are faced with the problem of constructing a non-trivial character, viz.,
L156@P4: the signum of the determinant, on the group of unitary operators in the
L157@P4: factor. This character must satisfy certain additional conditions if the determinant theory is to be at all reasonable. The following theorem demonstrates the impossibility of constructing a character satisfying the barest
L158@P4: minimum of such conditions.

L160@P4: the group of unitary operators in M, no character x with the property x(X U) =

L163@P4: continuous in the uniform topology.

L167@P4: equivalent projections with sum I.

L170@P4: generated by such operators is uniformly dense in Mn,.
